lessons.example: A runner covers 120 m in 8 s: v = 120 ÷ 8 = 15 m/s.
explanation: Speed is how much distance is covered in each second.
Divide the distance by the time taken.
The unit comes from the division: metres ÷ seconds = m/s.
lessons.tip: Average speed uses the whole journey, even the parts at rest.
lessons.title: Speed

lessons.example: Walk 3 m east then 3 m west in 2 s: distance 6 m, displacement 0, so average velocity is 0.
explanation: Speed has size only; velocity also has a direction.
Displacement is the straight line from start to finish, not the path walked.
A full circle brings you back to the start, so the displacement is zero.
lessons.tip: If a question says "returns to the start", the displacement is zero.
lessons.title: Velocity and displacement

lessons.example: From rest to 24 m/s in 8 s: a = (24 − 0) ÷ 8 = 3 m/s².
explanation: Acceleration is how much the velocity changes each second.
Take the change in velocity and divide by the time it took.
A negative answer means slowing down.
lessons.tip: "From rest" always means u = 0.
lessons.title: Acceleration

explanation: Start from the velocity you already have, then add what the acceleration adds.
Each second the velocity grows by another a metres per second.
Use it when the time is known but the distance is not.
lessons.tip: Check the unit: a × t is m/s² × s = m/s, which matches u.
lessons.title: Velocity–time equation

lessons.example: From rest with a = 2 m/s² for 5 s: s = 0 + ½(2)(25) = 25 m.
explanation: The first part, ut, is the distance the starting velocity alone would cover.
The second part, ½at², is the extra distance the acceleration adds.
Square the time before multiplying.
lessons.tip: Squaring the time is the step most answers get wrong.
lessons.title: Displacement equation

lessons.example: From rest, a = 3 m/s² over 24 m: v² = 0 + 2(3)(24) = 144, so v = 12 m/s.
explanation: Use this one when the time is not given.
Work out v² first, then take the square root at the very end.
lessons.tip: If the question gives a distance and no time, this is the equation.
lessons.title: Velocity–displacement equation

lessons.example: A book on a desk: weight down and the desk pushing up are equal, so it stays still.
explanation: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless a net force acts on it.
At rest it stays at rest; moving, it keeps the same velocity in a straight line.
Balanced forces are the same as no force at all.
lessons.formula: no net force → no change in motion
lessons.tip: Constant velocity means the forces are balanced, not that there are none.
lessons.title: Newton's first law

lessons.example: A 5 kg box accelerating at 2 m/s² needs F = 5 × 2 = 10 N.
explanation: A net force makes a mass accelerate.
Multiply the mass by the acceleration to get the force in newtons.
The same force gives a lighter object a bigger acceleration.
lessons.tip: Use the net force, after any friction has been taken off.
lessons.title: Newton's second law

lessons.arabic: لكل فعل رد فعل مساوٍ في المقدار مضاد في الاتجاه
lessons.example: A swimmer pushes the water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
explanation: Forces always come in pairs, on two different objects.
The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
They never cancel out, because they act on different bodies.
lessons.formula: every action has an equal, opposite reaction
lessons.tip: If a question says the pair cancels out, it is wrong: they act on different objects.
lessons.title: Newton's third law

lessons.example: A 6 kg bag weighs W = 6 × 10 = 60 N.
explanation: Weight is the force gravity pulls with, measured in newtons.
Multiply the mass in kilograms by g, which is about 10 N/kg on Earth.
Mass does not change on the Moon, but weight does.
lessons.tip: Mass is in kilograms, weight in newtons. Never mix them.
lessons.title: Weight and gravity

lessons.example: At 8 m/s around a circle of radius 4 m: a = 64 ÷ 4 = 16 m/s².
explanation: Something moving in a circle is always accelerating, because its direction keeps changing.
The acceleration points at the centre of the circle.
Square the speed, then divide by the radius.
lessons.tip: Twice the speed is four times the acceleration.
lessons.title: Circular motion

lessons.example: A 3 kg ball at 4 m/s has p = 3 × 4 = 12 kg·m/s.
explanation: Momentum measures how hard something is to stop.
Multiply the mass by the velocity; the unit is kg·m/s.
In a collision the total momentum stays the same.
lessons.tip: Momentum has a direction, so opposite motions can cancel.
lessons.title: Momentum

explanation: Friction opposes sliding between two surfaces.
Multiply the coefficient μ by the normal force N.
On a flat surface the normal force equals the weight.
lessons.tip: μ has no unit, so the answer is in newtons.
lessons.title: Friction

lessons.example: A 20 N push over 3 m does W = 20 × 3 = 60 J.
explanation: Work is done when a force moves something along its own direction.
Multiply the force by the distance moved; the unit is the joule.
No movement means no work, however hard you push.
lessons.tip: A force at right angles to the motion does no work.
lessons.title: Work

lessons.example: A 4 kg object at 3 m/s: KE = ½ × 4 × 9 = 18 J.
explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of movement.
Square the speed, multiply by the mass, then halve it.
Doubling the speed gives four times the energy.
lessons.tip: Square the speed before you multiply by the mass.
lessons.title: Kinetic energy

lessons.example: A 2 kg book 10 m up, with g = 10: PE = 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J.
explanation: Gravitational potential energy is the energy of height.
Multiply mass, g and height together.
Lose height and that energy turns into movement.
lessons.tip: Height is measured from whatever level the question calls zero.
lessons.title: Potential energy

lessons.example: Dropped from 10 m with g = 10: v = √(2 × 10 × 10) = √200 ≈ 14.1 m/s.
explanation: Energy is never lost, only moved from one form to another.
For a falling object, potential energy becomes kinetic energy.
The mass cancels, so v = √(2gh) whatever the object weighs.
lessons.tip: A heavy and a light ball dropped together land at the same speed.
lessons.title: Conservation of energy

explanation: Power is how quickly work is done.
Divide the work in joules by the time in seconds to get watts.
The same job done in half the time needs twice the power.
lessons.tip: Rearranged, W = Pt, which is how motor questions are usually set.
lessons.title: Power

lessons.example: 40 J useful from 50 J in: 40 ÷ 50 × 100 = 80%.
explanation: No machine turns all its energy into the job you want.
Divide the useful energy by the energy put in, then multiply by 100.
The rest usually leaves as heat.
lessons.tip: Efficiency can never be more than 100%.
lessons.title: Efficiency

explanation: A wave moves one wavelength forward in each cycle.
Multiply the frequency in hertz by the wavelength in metres.
In the same material the speed is fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
lessons.tip: Frequency and wavelength are inversely related at a fixed speed.
lessons.title: Wave equation

lessons.example: f = 50 Hz gives T = 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s.
explanation: The period is the time for one complete cycle.
Frequency is how many cycles happen each second.
Each is one divided by the other.
lessons.tip: A big frequency always means a small period.
lessons.title: Period and frequency

lessons.example: Making a pendulum four times longer changes T from 1 s to 2 s.
explanation: A pendulum swings back and forth in equal times.
The period depends on the length and on gravity, not on the mass.
Because of the square root, four times the length doubles the period.
lessons.tip: Adding a heavier bob does not change the period.
lessons.title: Simple harmonic motion

lessons.example: Light reaches us from the Sun through empty space; sound does not.
explanation: In a transverse wave the vibration is at right angles to the travel, like light.
In a longitudinal wave the vibration is along the travel, like sound in air.
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material, so it cannot cross a vacuum; light needs none.
lessons.tip: If a question mentions a vacuum, think about whether the wave needs matter.
lessons.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves

lessons.example: An echo returns in 2 s at 340 m/s: d = 340 × 2 ÷ 2 = 340 m.
explanation: An echo travels to the wall and back, so it covers twice the distance.
Multiply speed by time, then halve the answer.
lessons.key: Echo and the speed of sound
lessons.tip: Forgetting to halve is the usual mistake.
lessons.title: Echo and the speed of sound
lessons.topicTitle: Echo and the speed of sound

lessons.example: A siren sounds higher as the ambulance comes towards you and lower once it passes.
explanation: Movement between a source and a listener changes the frequency heard.
Coming closer squashes the waves, so the pitch rises.
Moving away stretches them, so the pitch falls.
lessons.tip: The source frequency itself never changes, only the frequency received.
lessons.title: The Doppler effect

lessons.example: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.
explanation: Reflection bounces light off a surface at the same angle it arrived.
Refraction bends light when it enters a material where it travels at a different speed.
Entering a denser material slows light and bends it towards the normal.
lessons.formula: light bends when its speed changes
lessons.tip: Light entering glass slows down and bends towards the normal.
lessons.title: Reflection and refraction

explanation: Current is the amount of charge passing a point each second.
Divide the charge in coulombs by the time in seconds to get amperes.
lessons.tip: One ampere is one coulomb per second.
lessons.title: Electric current

lessons.example: V = 100 V across R = 50 Ω: I = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 A.
explanation: Voltage pushes current through a resistance.
Rearrange to I = V/R for current, or R = V/I for resistance.
lessons.tip: Write the triangle V over I and R and cover what you need.
lessons.title: Ohm's law

lessons.example: 10 Ω and 20 Ω in series: R = 30 Ω.
explanation: In series there is only one path, so the resistances simply add.
The same current flows through every component.
The total is always bigger than the biggest single resistor.
lessons.tip: Series adds; parallel always gives less than the smallest.
lessons.title: Resistors in series

explanation: In parallel the current has more than one path, so the total resistance drops.
Add the reciprocals, then take the reciprocal of the answer.
The total is always smaller than the smallest resistor.
lessons.tip: If your answer is bigger than the smallest resistor, you forgot the last step.
lessons.title: Resistors in parallel

explanation: Power is the energy a component uses each second.
Multiply the voltage across it by the current through it.
lessons.tip: With Ohm’s law this also gives P = I²R and P = V²/R.
lessons.title: Electrical power

lessons.example: I = 3 A through R = 4 Ω: P = 9 × 4 = 36 W.
explanation: When you know the current and the resistance, square the current first.
Doubling the current gives four times the power.
lessons.tip: This is why thick cables are used for large currents.
lessons.title: Power and resistance

lessons.example: Moving two charges from 1 cm to 2 cm apart leaves a quarter of the force.
explanation: Two charges attract or repel along the line between them.
The force falls with the square of the distance.
Double the separation and the force drops to a quarter.
lessons.tip: An inverse square law: the distance is squared, not just doubled.
lessons.title: Coulomb's law

lessons.example: A 2 kW heater for 3 h uses 2 × 3 = 6 kWh.
explanation: Energy used is power multiplied by time.
In joules use seconds; in kilowatt-hours use kilowatts and hours.
lessons.tip: Watch the units: kWh needs hours, not seconds.
lessons.title: Electrical energy

explanation: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force.
Multiply the field strength, the current and the length in the field.
The force is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field.
lessons.tip: A wire along the field feels no force at all.
lessons.title: Force on a current

lessons.example: q = 2 C at 3 m/s in 4 T: F = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 N.
explanation: A charge moving across a magnetic field is pushed sideways.
Multiply the charge, its speed and the field strength.
A charge at rest feels no magnetic force.
lessons.tip: The force is at right angles to both the velocity and the field.
lessons.title: Force on a moving charge

lessons.example: Pushing a magnet into a coil makes the meter flick; holding it there reads zero.
explanation: Changing the magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage across it.
Faster movement, more turns or a stronger magnet all give a bigger voltage.
Nothing is induced while the magnet is held still.
lessons.formula: moving a magnet induces a voltage
lessons.tip: It is the change that matters, not the field itself.
lessons.title: Electromagnetic induction

lessons.example: Dropping a magnet through a copper tube takes longer than through a plastic one.
explanation: The induced current always flows so as to fight the change that caused it.
Push a north pole in and the coil presents a north pole back.
This is conservation of energy: you must do work to generate electricity.
lessons.formula: the induced current opposes the change
lessons.tip: If induction helped the change, energy would come from nowhere.
lessons.title: Lenz's law

explanation: A transformer changes voltage using two coils on one iron core.
The voltages are in the same ratio as the numbers of turns.
More turns on the secondary means a higher voltage out.
lessons.tip: Transformers only work on alternating current.
lessons.title: Transformers

lessons.example: A compass near a current-carrying wire turns to follow the circle.
explanation: A current makes a magnetic field in circles around the wire.
Point your right thumb along the current and your fingers curl the field way.
The field gets weaker further from the wire.
lessons.tip: Reverse the current and the field reverses too.
lessons.title: Magnetic field of a wire

lessons.example: Doubling the frequency doubles the energy of each photon.
explanation: Light comes in packets called photons.
A photon’s energy is Planck’s constant times the frequency.
Higher frequency light carries more energy per photon.
lessons.tip: Brightness changes how many photons arrive, not the energy of each one.
lessons.title: Photon energy

lessons.example: Red light on zinc releases nothing; dim ultraviolet releases electrons at once.
explanation: Light can knock electrons out of a metal surface.
Below a threshold frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light is.
This is evidence that light behaves as particles.
lessons.tip: Brighter light means more photons, not more energetic ones.
lessons.title: The photoelectric effect

lessons.example: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons but different numbers of neutrons.
explanation: An atom has protons and neutrons in a tiny nucleus, with electrons around it.
The number of protons is the atomic number and names the element.
Change the neutrons and you get an isotope of the same element.
lessons.tip: Isotopes of an element behave the same chemically.
lessons.title: Atomic structure

lessons.example: 100 g with a 5-day half-life, after 15 days: 3 half-lives, so 100 → 50 → 25 → 12.5 g.
explanation: A half-life is the time for half the radioactive nuclei to decay.
Count how many half-lives have passed, then halve that many times.
lessons.tip: Divide the total time by the half-life to get the number of halvings.
lessons.title: Half-life

lessons.example: Uranium-238 alpha decays to thorium-234: the mass number falls by 4.
explanation: Alpha decay throws out 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the mass number drops by 4.
Beta decay turns a neutron into a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1.
Gamma is energy only and changes neither number.
lessons.tip: Alpha changes both numbers, beta only the proton number, gamma neither.
lessons.title: Nuclear decay

lessons.example: A little mass is lost in every fusion reaction and appears as energy.
explanation: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing.
Because c² is enormous, a tiny mass holds a huge amount of energy.
This is where the energy of the Sun comes from.
lessons.tip: c is 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so c² is about 9 × 10¹⁶.
lessons.title: Mass and energy

lessons.example: Particles in accelerators get very close to c but never reach it.
explanation: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer.
Pushing a mass faster needs more and more energy as it approaches that speed.
Reaching it would need infinite energy, so nothing with mass can.
lessons.formula: nothing with mass reaches the speed of light
lessons.tip: Only massless things, such as photons, travel at c.
lessons.title: Relativity
